subject: Cognitive Science
title: Task Switching Costs
description: A quick, practical guide to Task Switching Costs.

hook.text: Switch from writing an email to answering a question. That tiny pause? It's your brain reconfiguring.

buildup.text: Jersild discovered switch costs in 1927. Alternating between two tasks is slower than doing each in a block.

discovery.text: The cost comes from loading new mental rules. Each task has a 'task set' the brain must activate.

twist.text: Even when you know the switch is coming, you can't fully prepare. Some cost is unavoidable.

climax.text: Residual switch cost means traces of the previous task linger, slowing you on the new one.

punchline.text: Every switch leaves a ghost of the last task behind.

quiz.question: What causes task-switching costs?
options: Loading new mental rules for each task

details.summary: When switching between tasks, the brain needs time to deactivate the old task set and activate the new one. This switch cost is measured in hundreds of milliseconds per switch and accumulates with frequency. Residual interference from the previous task further slows performance.
details.whyItMatters: Switch costs explain why interruptions are so disruptive. Even brief email checks during deep work impose measurable cognitive costs that extend well beyond the interruption itself.
takeaways: Task switching requires reconfiguring mental task sets
Each switch adds hundreds of milliseconds of delay
Residual interference from the previous task persists

faq.question: What is a task set in cognitive science?
faq.answer: A task set is the mental configuration needed for a specific task, including relevant rules, response mappings, and attentional settings. Switching tasks requires dismantling the current set and building a new one, which takes measurable time and resources.

faq.question: Can preparation reduce switch costs?
faq.answer: Advance warning of an upcoming switch reduces but never eliminates the cost. A residual switch cost remains even with ample preparation time, suggesting part of the reconfiguration can only happen after the new task stimulus actually appears.
